item.title: MiBeeNvr: From v0.1.0 to v0.13.1
item.description: MiBeeNvr is an NVR built for a home camera fleet. v0.1.0 shipped on May 6, 2026; v0.13.1 on October 19 — thirteen releases in a bit over five months. This post merges the per-release notes from v0.1.0 through v0.13.1 into one timeline: what each step did, and why. The house style for mechanisms is plain words first, then a picture, then the parameters. The v0.13.0 performance benchmarks are a separate post, linked at the end.

item.title: One UI for Many Hosts? A Survey of the Incus Web UI Ecosystem
item.description:
The CLI covers the cluster’s needs, but “open a browser and see every machine” never goes away. I went through the Incus-related web UI ecosystem and layered it by “how many hosts can it manage”. Conclusion up front: taking “manage multiple independent clusters” and “one-click cross-cluster migration” together, no maintained open-source project does both.

The official UI’s boundary first

Incus itself ships no web UI. The official adaptation, incus-ui-canonical (a rebrand of the LXD UI), is served by incusd itself at 8443/ui — same origin — which creates a structural limit:

item.title: One UI for Multiple Clusters: What Open Source Offers
item.description:
The requirement grew: two independent clusters, one per subnet (each starting with a single leader, replicas to follow), one web frontend above both, plus one-click cross-cluster migration. This post separates “intra-cluster migration” from “cross-cluster migration” — they are not the same thing at all — and covers the five hard constraints of going cross-cluster, plus what the open-source survey concluded.

Pinning the topology down

Three layers: a single web frontend at the top (incus-hub / the control plane); below it two clusters sharing nothing — cluster A on subnet 1 (192.168.10.0/24, leader A1 + replica A2) and cluster B on subnet 2 (192.168.20.0/24, leader B1 + replica B2), each internally shaped like the “1 leader + N replicas” from earlier posts. The orange dashed line is cross-cluster migration: copy + delete in essence, with an IP change guaranteed. There is no shared database between the clusters; profiles, networks, and pool definitions are disconnected — that fact creates every difficulty below.

item.title: MiBeeHive: The "Hive" Toolbox I Built for My Studio
item.description: Coming from an operations background, later transitioning to development, the number of projects I maintain keeps growing. Various middleware, databases, monitoring components… each version upgrade is a manual labor: go to the official site to find the download link, compare version numbers, manually download to the internal network, then distribute to each machine. I used to write a bunch of Shell scripts to periodically pull the latest versions to the LAN — functional but not user-friendly: scripts scattered everywhere, adding new software required writing parsing logic by hand, and there was nothing to check when things went wrong.

item.title: MiBeeSteward: From v0.1.0 to v0.8.0
item.description: MiBeeSteward is the device management and monitoring system I wrote for my own studio: one Go binary stringing network-device discovery, classification, monitoring, and management into a single line. v0.1.0 shipped on July 5, 2026; v0.8.0 landed on October 24 — eight minor releases and three patches evolving a “single-subnet scanner” into “a distributed system that passes enterprise audits”, then moving discovery into the router and probing out to the public egress. Each version used to have its own post; this one merges the v0.1.0–v0.8.0 release records into a single timeline: what each step did, and why.

item.title: MiBeeSteward v0.9.0: Phones Come and Go — the Asset Archive Remembers
item.description: The most numerous devices on a network aren’t servers — they’re phones, and the most transient ones too: on the office WiFi at nine in the morning, gone by six, absent all weekend. A phone upgrade leaves the old handset behind, never to connect again; a guest’s phone visited once, and never again. The old handling was blunt: offline past a threshold, the sweeper deleted the row, history included — and when the same phone ever connected again, it was a “new device”, with nothing to connect it to the last seen time, the old IP, the services it once ran.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.6.0's Test Machines: Three Camera Projects Updated in Sync
item.description: The concurrently released MiBeeNvr v0.6.0 brought major features like timelapse, video transcoding, and ONVIF enhancements. Unit tests alone are far from enough — the full workflow must be tested against real camera hardware. To provide reliable test machines for this release, three camera projects were updated on the same day, June 5th — both to supply testing environments for the NVR and to solve some typical embedded development engineering problems along the way.

item.title: Taking Over onvif-go: Real-Camera Fixes, Zero Dependencies, and Service Facades
item.description:
MiBeeNvr talks to cameras over ONVIF, and this library is what sits underneath. ONVIF is the de facto standard for IP video surveillance equipment: device discovery, media profiles, PTZ control, event subscriptions — all one set of SOAP-over-HTTP service conventions. Any brand that claims ONVIF compliance can, in theory, be integrated through the same calls.

onvif-go is that stack implemented in Go. We did not write it from scratch: its upstream was 0x524a/onvif-go — the previous author reshaped it into its modern form of a client plus a virtual camera server (the git history still traces back to earlier Go ONVIF attempts in the community). But upstream stalled entering 2026: the last merged PR landed in mid-January, the v1.0-through-v1.1.3 release cadence from late 2025 never resumed, and three Improve Test Coverage issues filed in November 2025 sit unclaimed to this day. Meanwhile we hit two problems in our own camera pool that could only be fixed inside the library.

item.title: Where Should MiBeeSteward Live: Router Form vs Host Form, a Controlled Comparison
item.description: MiBee Steward is an open-source network device management system (a single Go binary handling automatic discovery, identification, and the ledger of LAN devices) with three deployment shapes: directly on the router, on an ordinary host in the network, or one center with several lightweight agents covering multiple subnets. This time, on one physical network, all three shapes were compared under the same version and parameters — environment, process, and data laid out to answer “where should it live”.

item.title: Four Protocol Libraries, Extracted: ONVIF and GB28181 in Go and Rust
item.description:
MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols. ONVIF is the de facto standard internationally — Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, and Bosch all speak it. GB/T 28181 is China’s national surveillance standard, unavoidable in government and state-owned projects. The device side (Raspberry Pi camera firmware, one Go and one Rust implementation) and the NVR side (MiBeeNvr, Go) both speak these two protocols, and the stacks have always lived inside the projects.

Two problems with that. First, this code is pickled in interop details — digest-auth qop handling, SIP Via-branch uniqueness, MANSCDP element-vs-attribute dual forms, TCP framing header byte counts — each one was ground out against a real platform, and a new project would have to grind them all again. Second, a library survey two weeks ago showed the open-source landscape for these protocols is unevenly populated; several positions have no one standing in them.

item.title: MiBee Release Log: Four Repos Tagged the Same Day
item.description:
On September 20, 2026, four repositories tagged releases on the same day — and they each happen to cover one stretch of the chain:

  • See what’s on the network — MiBeeSteward v0.6.0
  • Get your homemade camera recognized — onvif-c v0.1.0
  • Record the footage and play it back anytime — MiBeeNvr v0.13.0-preview.1
  • Have someone take notes on the serial console while you debug firmware — serialtap v0.1.0

The first two are routine iterations of existing projects; the last two are tagging v0.1.0 for the first time. What’s worth playing with in each release — and why it was built that way.

item.title: The Protocol Library Family Grows to Five: onvif-go Reaches v2 and the GB28181 Device Side Wraps Up
item.description: MiBee’s camera access runs on two protocols: ONVIF, the de facto standard internationally that Hikvision, Axis, and Dahua all speak, and GB/T 28181, China’s national surveillance standard that government and state-owned projects cannot avoid. The protocol stack is open-sourced as five independent libraries split by protocol × language × role, all extracted from production code, and in the latest release round all five tagged on the same day: onvif-go entered the stable v2 line, onvif-device-rs shipped to crates.io, gb28181-go and gb28181-rs closed out the 2022 device-side surface, and onvif-c debuted as the fifth member. This post goes library by library through capability boundaries, key design decisions, and remaining limitations, stated as released.

item.title: MiBeeNvr v0.13.0 Performance Self-Benchmark: Capacity and Resource Curves on Three Hardware Tiers
item.description:
Choosing an NVR keeps running into the same wall: there are no public performance numbers with stated measurement conditions. Third-party cross-product benchmarks don’t exist; what you can find is either vendor-quoted partial metrics (detector inference latency, say) or editorial estimate tables that omit the hardware, bitrate, and framerate conditions — the numbers can’t be compared against each other.

So I measured MiBeeNvr’s own capacity and resource curves: three hardware tiers, recording ramps from 16 to 68 cameras, concurrent playback on top of full load, pure forwarding, an fsync-policy comparison, plus a read-only observation of a 7×24 production machine. The methodology, pass/fail criteria, and test scripts are all published with this post. The goal is not to rank products — with no comparable public methodology, ranking means nothing — but to answer two questions that actually come up during capacity planning: how many cameras a machine of a given tier can carry, and whether the bottleneck lands on CPU, memory, or storage.

item.title: onvif-go Tutorial: Connect Cameras, Pretend to Be One, Test Your NVR
item.description: onvif-go is the library that plays the “connect to cameras” role in MiBee’s camera-access stack: when your program needs to discover, authenticate, pull streams from, or control a camera over ONVIF — or pretend to be a camera so an NVR can connect to it — this is the one. It ships both roles, client and virtual-camera server, and its compatibility matrix (Hikvision, Axis, Dahua, Bosch, Amcrest, HiSilicon OEMs, a minimal ESP32 implementation) was fed by real packet captures. MiBeeNvr runs its ONVIF access on this library.

item.title: gb28181-go Tutorial: From Device Registration to Platform Ingest
item.description: gb28181-go is the only all-in-one volume among the five protocol libraries: the same module carries the device side (UAC, registering a media source to a GB/T 28181 platform) and the platform side (UAS, accepting device registrations and pulling streams from them). The device code came out of the MiBee Eye Raspberry Pi camera firmware, and the platform side was extracted wholesale from MiBeeNvr’s GB28181 access implementation — the two ends bite against each other in production every day.

item.title: gb28181-rs Tutorial: Registering a Device to a GB28181 Platform in Rust
item.description: gb28181-rs is the Rust implementation of the GB/T 28181 device side (UAC): register a media source to a national-standard platform, push streams to it, and receive platform-pushed controls. It is a twin of gb28181-go — the same responsibilities in two languages, with PTZ bit decoding, talk-back SDP, and snapshots sharing one set of golden wire-format tables, so whichever packaging drifts turns red first. The library was extracted from MiBee’s Rust camera firmware and runs in production daily.

item.title: onvif-device-rs Tutorial: Building an ONVIF Camera in Rust
item.description: onvif-device-rs covers the other half of ONVIF: where onvif-go is “connect to cameras,” this library is “be the camera” — it makes an NVR discover your device, read its information, pull its stream, drive its PTZ, and receive its events, all over ONVIF. Use it to turn a Linux board or an industrial PC into an ONVIF camera, to build test fixtures for NVR development, or to bring a PC webcam into an NVR. It fills the previously empty slot of an ONVIF device-side implementation in Rust, extracted verbatim from MiBee’s Raspberry Pi camera firmware with byte-stable responses interoperating against MiBeeNvr byte for byte.

item.title: onvif-c Tutorial: Adding an ONVIF Device to Your ESP32 Firmware
item.description: onvif-c is the most “physical” of the five protocol libraries: a plain C ONVIF device component for ESP-IDF with a footprint around 10KB and zero third-party dependencies. When an ESP32 camera firmware needs to be discovered by an NVR, answer device-information queries, hand out stream URIs, and report motion events — this one component covers it. There is no XML parser inside: action recognition is strstr(), responses are assembled with snprintf(), and the memory model is simple enough to call safely from sensor callback context. The four MiBee camera firmware repos carry it in lockstep, and library changes go through real hardware before release.

item.title: RuView, Taken Apart: the Repo, the Hardware Paths, the Model Shelf, and the Ecosystem
item.description: 92k stars on GitHub — RuView is the most-watched open-source project in WiFi sensing: an ESP32 mesh captures CSI, a Rust server does fusion and learning, and pose, vital signs, room fingerprints, and occupancy counts all come out of the radio, under MIT. The author is ruvnet (the creator of claude-flow), and the repository root contains .claude-flow, .swarm, and CLAUDE.md — this is a project developed at scale by AI agents, an identity that will matter repeatedly below.

item.title: Adaptive Recording and Storage Design in MiBeeNvr
item.description: Outside writeups of MiBeeNvr’s adaptive recording mostly stop at “motion-aware, saves disk”: what signal drives the gating, why the switch loses no frames, and which cameras it fails on rarely get covered. This post takes all three apart — plain words first, then a picture, then the parameters, with a full glossary at the end. Mechanism descriptions are based on the v0.13.0 documentation and release records (October 2026); the version-by-version timeline is in MiBeeNvr: From v0.1.0 to v0.13.1.

item.title: MiBeeNvr's Recording Deep-Check and Full-Link Observability
item.description: The nastiest failures in a surveillance pipeline are the ones that never raise an error. A frozen live tile could be a dropped camera, network jitter, or the NVR itself — before v0.12, the available diagnostic tools were reading logs and counting frames. The recording side was worse off: ingest, muxing, and writes all reported success, yet playback would corrupt from some point onward, and the write path never said a word about it.

item.title: MiBeeNvr Release Log: Store Ships 0.13.1 While the Repo Reaches 0.14.1
item.description: On October 30, MiBeeNvr’s two distribution channels each took a step on the same day: the GitHub repo tagged v0.14.1, and the fnOS app store finished reviewing and publishing v0.13.1. Back in late September the store onboarding application hadn’t even gotten a reply (noted in the previous release log); this time review plus publication landed within one day, which caught me off guard. The catch: the approved version now trails the repo by two — 0.14.0 and 0.14.1 have yet to reach the store.
